subsection: 3. Gender socialisation and its impact on participation

notes.b: Gender socialisation shapes which activities young people see as open to them. To understand why boys and girls take part in sport differently, start with how children learn what is expected of them.
points: Socialisation is the lifelong process of learning the norms (the unwritten rules about how to act), values and behaviour expected in a society. It goes on throughout life, not only in childhood.

Gender socialisation is the part of that learning that tells you what is seen as appropriate for boys and men, and for girls and women. This is why a child may rule out an activity before ever trying it.

notes.b: An agent of socialisation is a person or group that passes these expectations on. Each agent below teaches children, often without meaning to, which activities suit their sex.
points: Family: the toys children are given, the activities encouraged and the behaviour praised. Children learn what earns approval at home.
Peers (friends of the same age): they reward behaviour that fits gender norms and mock behaviour that does not, so children copy what their friends accept.
School: the activities offered and the expectations teachers hold. What is on offer, and who is expected to do it, tells pupils what is normal.
Media: the images of male and female athletes that young people see. There is more on this in Gender, media and body image.
Sports clubs and coaches: the activities offered and the language used with boys and girls.
Religion and culture: the roles and behaviour a community treats as proper for each sex.
notes.tip: Name the agent and say what it does, for example family through toys, activities encouraged and praise, or school through activities offered and teacher expectations.

notes.h: Examples of gender socialisation in sport
notes.b: These everyday examples show socialisation at work: small differences in what children are given and told add up to different sporting habits.
points: Boys are given footballs and encouraged to be rough and competitive, so they learn that sport and aggression suit boys.
Girls are given dance classes and praised for being neat and graceful, so they learn that looking good while moving is what is expected of girls.
Comments such as 'throws like a girl' teach children that some physical skills belong to one sex, and that doing them 'like a girl' is an insult.

notes.h: Social regulation of the body: definition and history
notes.b: Society does not only teach roles, it also sets rules about bodies. Social regulation of the body is the idea that these rules decide which physical activity people feel they may take part in, and the past shows this clearly for women.
points: Social regulation of the body is the way society, through its norms, expectations, rules and media images, defines how bodies should look, move and behave.
This regulation determines which physical activity people feel is appropriate or available to them, so it limits participation before a person has even chosen.
In the past, women were historically excluded or restricted, for example barred from some events and clubs.
In the past, women's competition distances were limited and dress rules restricted their participation.
In the past, a belief that strenuous exercise harmed women's health discouraged women from taking part.
Women's boxing was first included in the Olympic Games in 2012, in London, which shows how recently some barriers were lifted.
notes.tip: If asked what social regulation of the body is, define it using norms, expectations, rules and media images, then link it to which activity people feel is appropriate or available. For the past, give examples of exclusion and restriction for women.

notes.h: Social regulation of the body today
notes.b: The old formal bans have largely gone, but the regulation continues in softer forms that still affect who takes part and in what.
points: Dress codes and kit expectations set out what women and men should wear to take part, so people who dislike or feel uneasy in the required kit may stay away.
Muscular women, and men who take part in activities seen as feminine, are judged or criticised, which punishes people who step outside the norm.
Unequal provision (the facilities, teams and opportunities offered) and unequal pay for women's sport persist.
Appearance expectations continue to shape which activities people feel comfortable taking part in. There is more on this in Gender, media and body image.
notes.tip: Discuss the effect on both men and women, not only women. Use the present-day examples here for the continuing part of the question.

notes.h: Effects of social regulation on women and men
notes.b: Social regulation does not affect only one sex. It pushes women and men towards different activities, and each group pays a price.
points: For women: girls are steered away from contact, power and strength sports and from visible muscle, because these are not seen as suited to women.
For women: self-surveillance, meaning constantly monitoring and judging their own appearance, takes attention away from enjoying the activity.
For women: these pressures contribute to drop-out (giving up sport) in adolescence.
For men: pressure to be strong, tough and competitive, whether or not they want to be.
For men: avoidance of dance, gymnastics and synchronised swimming, which are seen as feminine.
For men: pressure to play through pain and injury, rather than stop and look after themselves.
For men: reluctance to show weakness or seek help.
notes.tip: A question on how social regulation affects participation expects both men and women, so give effects for each.

notes.b: Hegemonic means dominant and widely accepted. Hegemonic masculinity is the ideal of manhood that a society holds up above all others, and it sets a standard that boys and men are judged against.
points: Hegemonic masculinity is the dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a man in a society, treated as the norm against which men are measured.
It is a standard that individual men are measured against; it does not describe all men, so many men do not match it.
The concept was developed by the sociologist (a researcher who studies society) R. W. Connell.
Characteristics: physical strength, toughness, aggression, competitiveness, dominance, emotional restraint (not showing feelings), risk-taking and heterosexuality (attraction to women).
notes.tip: Do not write that hegemonic masculinity means all men. It means the dominant, widely accepted ideal. When asked to explain it, give the definition and the characteristics.

notes.h: Hegemonic masculinity: impact on boys and girls
notes.b: Because this ideal links manhood with strength and toughness, it rewards some boys, penalises others, and also changes how girls are seen when they play sport.
points: For boys: boys who fit the ideal gain high status in contact team sports, which rewards them for matching the ideal.
For boys: boys who are less sporty or prefer aesthetic activities (ones where how movement looks matters, such as dance) are excluded or ridiculed.
For boys: boys are encouraged to play through injury and violence, because toughness is part of the ideal.
For boys: boys who do not fit the ideal may drop out of sport.
For girls: sport itself is defined as masculine, so girls who play are seen as less feminine.
For girls: women's sport is treated as second-rate.
notes.tip: Always answer for both boys and girls. Pick characteristics such as strength, toughness or competitiveness and explain how each affects participation.

notes.b: Alongside the ideal man there is an ideal woman. Hegemonic femininity is the matching standard for girls and women, and it points them towards different activities.
points: Hegemonic femininity is the dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a woman in a society, treated as the norm against which women are measured.
It is a standard that individual women are measured against; it does not describe all women.
Characteristics: slimness, grace, attractiveness and an appearance focus, gentleness, passivity (taking a quiet, receptive role) and non-aggression, caring and deference (giving way to others).
notes.tip: Hegemonic means dominant and widely accepted, not all women. You may be asked to identify two characteristics and explain why they might affect girls' participation, so link each one to a sporting effect.

notes.h: Hegemonic femininity: impact on girls and boys
notes.b: The ideal of femininity affects girls most directly, but it also shapes what boys feel able to do.
points: For girls: activities that are aggressive, muscular, sweaty or contact-based seem unfeminine, so girls avoid them or drop out.
For girls: an emphasis on appearance leads to self-consciousness (worry about being watched and judged) about how they look while taking part.
For girls: they are channelled into aesthetic activities, such as dance or gymnastics, which fit the ideal of grace.
For boys: activities linked to femininity, such as dance and gymnastics, are avoided for fear of ridicule.
notes.tip: Both ideals affect both boys and girls, so cover both in your answer. Higher Level questions can ask you to explain hegemonic masculinity and hegemonic femininity together.

notes.b: Gender norms are learned, so they can be changed. These steps help boys and girls choose activities freely.
points: Visible role models who break stereotypes, such as women playing rugby, boxing and Gaelic games, and men taking part in dance, show young people that these activities are open to everyone.
Equal provision and media coverage for women's and men's sport, so women's sport is no longer treated as second-rate.
Mixed and choice-based PE (physical education), so boys and girls can choose activities without gender labels.
Coaches and teachers who challenge stereotyped comments as they happen, so comments like 'throws like a girl' do not go unchallenged.

keyTerms.definition: The lifelong process of learning the norms, values and behaviour that a society expects of its members.
The process of learning what is seen as appropriate for boys and men, and for girls and women.
The people and institutions, such as family, peers, school and media, that teach individuals a society's norms.
The way a society's norms, expectations, rules and media images define how bodies should look, move and behave.
The dominance of one set of ideas or values that most people accept as natural.
The dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a man, treated as the norm against which men are measured.
The dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a woman, treated as the norm against which women are measured.
An accepted standard of behaviour that a society expects its members to follow.
A fixed, oversimplified belief about what people of a particular group are like.
The habit of constantly monitoring and judging one's own appearance against social expectations.

questions.prompt: Explain hegemonic femininity and hegemonic masculinity, and why each might impact on the participation of boys and girls.
questions.model: Hegemonic masculinity is the dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a man in a society, treated as the norm against which men are measured. Its characteristics include physical strength, toughness, aggression, competitiveness, dominance, emotional restraint, risk-taking and heterosexuality. Because contact team sports reward these traits, boys who fit gain status, while boys who are less sporty or prefer aesthetic activities may be excluded or ridiculed, and boys may be pushed to play through injury or drop out. Girls are also affected: sport itself is defined as masculine, so girls who play are seen as less feminine, and women's sport is treated as second-rate. Hegemonic femininity is the dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a woman, treated as the norm against which women are measured. Its characteristics include slimness, grace, attractiveness, an appearance focus, gentleness, passivity, non-aggression, caring and deference. Activities that are aggressive, muscular, sweaty or contact-based seem unfeminine, so girls avoid them or drop out, and an emphasis on appearance brings self-consciousness. Girls are channelled into aesthetic activities such as dance. Boys are affected too: activities linked to femininity, such as dance and gymnastics, are avoided for fear of ridicule, which narrows their choices.

questions.prompt: Discuss how social regulation of the body impacts on the participation levels of men and women in physical activity.
questions.model: Social regulation of the body is the way society, through its norms, expectations, rules and media images, defines how bodies should look, move and behave, which shapes the activities people feel are appropriate or available to them. Historically, women were excluded or restricted: they were barred from some events and clubs, competition distances were limited, dress rules applied, and a belief that strenuous exercise harmed women's health discouraged them from taking part. Women's boxing was first included in the Olympic Games in 2012, in London. Today, dress codes and kit expectations, judgement of muscular women or of men in feminine activities, and unequal provision and pay for women's sport continue to limit participation. For women, girls are steered away from contact, power and strength sports and from visible muscle, women practise self-surveillance of their appearance, and these pressures contribute to drop-out in adolescence. For men, the pressure to be strong, tough and competitive leads to avoidance of dance, gymnastics and synchronised swimming, pressure to play through pain and injury, and reluctance to show weakness or seek help. Women's participation is therefore narrowed by exclusion and appearance pressure, and men's by expectations of toughness.

questions.prompt: Explain hegemonic masculinity and give one way it can affect boys' participation in sport.
questions.model: Hegemonic masculinity is the dominant, widely accepted idea of what it means to be a man in a society, treated as the norm against which men are measured. It is a standard rather than a description of every man, and it includes physical strength, toughness, aggression, competitiveness and emotional restraint. One way it affects boys' participation: boys who do not fit the ideal, for example those who are less sporty or prefer dance, may be excluded or ridiculed by peers, which may lead them to drop out of sport altogether.
